title: A Body Plan Unlike Our Own
paragraphs: An octopus is built differently from almost any animal we know, and its circulation is a good example. That makes it one of the strangest bodies in the animal kingdom. It has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen, while the third sends that oxygen-rich blood around the rest of the body. Its blood is blue, because it relies on a copper-based protein to carry oxygen, whereas human blood uses an iron-based one.

The nervous system is just as unusual. Roughly two thirds of an octopus's neurons are located in its arms rather than in its central brain. As a result, each arm can explore, grasp and react with a high degree of independence. This arrangement helps the animal react quickly. Some researchers even describe the animal as having nine brains, although that phrase is a simplification.

Such figures vary between sources, so they are best read as approximate. What remains clear is that the octopus solves everyday problems with a body plan very unlike our own. Scientists keep studying octopuses because their bodies suggest that intelligence can evolve in very different ways.
